strengths: The paper addresses a clean and practically motivated question: when heterogeneous node weights must be incorporated into decentralized gradient tracking, does it matter whether weights are folded into the losses (Strategy I, doubly stochastic mixing) or into a row-stochastic mixing matrix with stationary distribution λ/n (Strategy II)? Prior work treats both as equivalent in expected descent direction, so the systematic head-to-head comparison fills a genuine gap.

The L²(λ;ℝᵈ) framework is a natural and elegant analytical device: it makes the λ-induced row-stochastic matrix self-adjoint (via detailed balance), enabling exact spectral analysis, while revealing the non-normality penalty (κ_λ, λ_max factors) for the doubly stochastic design. The recovery of the classical linear-speedup rate (Corollary 6.6) is a good sanity check.

The proof chain is complete and fairly self-contained: closed-form spectral norms of the recursion matrix via Kronecker factorization (Proposition B.14), accumulated consensus errors (Proposition 6.4), and end-to-end convergence rates (Theorem 6.5) with explicit constants, all with derivations shown in the appendix.

The translation from spectral conditions to interpretable topology/degree–weight constraints (Theorems 7.2, Corollary 7.3) and the practical Algorithm 2 (degree ∝ λ graph construction with fallbacks) connect theory to actionable design, and the experiments (synthetic least squares plus ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 across six topologies, multiple seeds) support the qualitative conclusion that Strategy II can win even with a smaller spectral gap, including on the tailor-made graphs.

Limitations of the Euclidean framework are discussed explicitly (Section 6.4), and the experiments are documented in enough detail (topologies, weight vectors, seeds, hyperparameters) to be largely reproducible.
weaknesses: Claims of novelty and tightness are overstated. Analyzing reversible Markov chains in the stationary-measure-weighted inner product is textbook material (Levin & Peres, cited by the authors themselves), so presenting L²(λ;ℝᵈ) as a fundamentally 'new analytical framework' is oversold. Similarly, the claim that 'Euclidean analysis leads to strictly looser bounds' is only demonstrated against one specific coarse rescaling argument (Eq. 8), not against the best possible Euclidean-space analysis; no lower bounds establish that the authors' own bounds are tight, so Q1 is answered only in a limited sense.

The central claim that the penalty terms κ_λ² and λ_max² are fundamental rather than artifacts of a particular upper-bound analysis is never substantiated by a lower bound or an instance showing Strategy I provably cannot achieve Strategy II's constants. The 'provably outperform' narrative rests on comparing one specific doubly stochastic matrix (lazy MH with λ≡1) against one specific row-stochastic construction on the same graph; the design freedom of the doubly stochastic matrix under heterogeneous weights is not explored.

The theory produces very crude constants (factors of 60, 62, 27, etc. from repeated Young/Jensen-type steps, and the loose supremum yielding η₁ = 0.1 in Theorem 7.1), which weakens the practical bite of the head-to-head convergence comparison in Section 7; the gap between the bounds and the consistently large experimental separations suggests the bounds are far from tight.

Experiments are limited in scale (n = 16 nodes) and scope: no comparison against existing heterogeneous-weight or push/row-stochastic baselines (e.g., exact diffusion, Liang et al. 2025a), no step-size tuning ablation clarifying whether the same α is fair for both strategies (a key confound given the claimed step-size advantage), and Assumption 6.2 assumes identical variance υ² across nodes, which sidesteps the heterogeneous noise likely present in practice.

Presentation issues reduce readability: dense theorem statements with opaque constants, notable typos ('existing lectures', 'obatin', 'definited', 'comparsion'), and an appendix where the Strategy I consensus proof is sketched as 'purely mechanical... omitted for brevity', which weakens full verifiability of the parallel result. A code artifact is referenced but no release is explicitly stated.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and previously underexplored question: how heterogeneous node weights should be incorporated in decentralized learning, and whether row-stochastic mixing can outperform doubly stochastic mixing.

The geometric observation is clean and clearly presented: under the λ-weighted inner product, the λ-induced row-stochastic matrix becomes self-adjoint (via the detailed-balance/symmetrization transform), while the doubly stochastic matrix incurs a distortion factor κλ, which the authors trace through the convergence bounds.

The derivation chain is complete: descent lemmas, consensus-error recursions with closed-form spectral norm computations (Proposition B.14), final rates (Theorem 6.5), a spectral comparison condition (Theorem 7.1), a topology-level condition (Corollary 7.3), and a practical degree-allocation algorithm (Algorithm 2) — the results connect to each other coherently.

Experiments cover a synthetic least-squares task and ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 training across multiple topologies (ring, grid, exponential, ER, geometric, and weight-tailored graphs), with the empirical observation that Strategy II can win even when its spectral gap is smaller, consistent with the theory.
The paper is honest about the degenerate uniform-weight case (Corollary 6.6 recovering the classical 1/√(nT) linear speedup), supporting internal consistency of the framework.
weaknesses: The central claim — that row-stochastic mixing 'provably outperforms' doubly stochastic mixing — is established only by comparing upper bounds with different constant factors, not by showing an actual convergence-rate separation or lower bound. Both strategies share the same asymptotic rate O(1/T), and the comparison hinges on loose constants (e.g., factors of 60, 27, κλ, λmax) in non-asymptotic upper bounds. A constant-factor comparison of loose upper bounds does not constitute proof that Strategy II converges faster on any instance; no lower-bound or instance-level separation argument is provided.

The claimed tightness of the L²(λ) framework is partially overstated because the Euclidean baseline in Section 6.4 / Eq. (8) is a strawman: it is obtained by a coarse rescaling of smoothness and noise (λmaxβ, λmax²υ²), whereas a more careful Euclidean analysis (e.g., using the weighted-average gradient tracking identity already available in Section 4.1) could avoid several of these λmax factors. The 'strictly looser Euclidean bounds' conclusion therefore conflates the geometry with weaknesses of one particular (conservative) prior analysis.

The core technical device — analyzing a reversible Markov chain via the similarity transform D^{1/2}WD^{-1/2} under a weighted inner product — is a textbook technique in Markov chain and spectral graph theory, and the related-work section itself notes that diffusion-style methods already handle heterogeneous weights via row-stochastic mixing (Sayed, 2014). The novelty is thus an incremental repackaging applied to gradient tracking, rather than a fundamentally new framework.

The comparison between strategies is entangled with the choice of mixing matrices: Strategy I is run with Wds on the given graph, while Strategy II uses a Metropolis–Hastings matrix with laziness parameter ε (set to 0.3 in experiments, vs. the more standard 0.5 used in prior work). Differences in experiments may partly reflect matrix construction choices rather than the intrinsic geometric penalty the paper attributes them to.

The experiments are limited in scale and rigor: n = 16 nodes only, two arbitrary random weight vectors, no statistical significance testing, loss/gradient-norm curves without confidence bands, and no step-size tuning per strategy — the theoretical step-size advantage of Strategy II is not isolated experimentally. The metric for the synthetic experiment (weighted average gradient norm at local iterates) does not exactly match the theoretical objective.

Theorem 7.1's proof assumes zero initialization errors and a shared step size, and its sufficient condition is derived from the same loose constant comparisons; the practical scope of the 'topology-design guideline' (degrees proportional to weights) is only validated on small graphs, and the necessity/sufficiency claim of Theorem 7.2 rests on spectral-gap identities whose edge cases (e.g., |σmin(W)| vs |σ2(W)|) deserve more care.

Presentation quality is below standard for a main-track submission: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('commonly used in existing lectures', 'obatin', 'definited', 'comparision', 'we can obatin'), inconsistent notation, and some displayed equations with dense, hard-to-parse constants. There is no explicit limitations section discussing scope (e.g., undirected graphs only, smooth nonconvex losses, no communication constraints).

Reproducibility is not adequately supported in the manuscript: the text refers to 'the code' in passing, but no repository link or artifact is provided in the visible material, and several experimental details (seed handling, per-topology hyperparameters) are only partially specified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored question: whether row-stochastic mixing with a prescribed stationary distribution can outperform doubly stochastic mixing when node weights are heterogeneous. Prior work (diffusion/Sayed; exact diffusion) handles both strategies but does not compare their rates, so the head-to-head analysis fills a real gap.

The weighted Hilbert-space framework L^2(λ; R^d) is a clean and well-motivated analytical device: the descent lemma naturally produces λ-weighted norms, and the self-adjointness of the λ-reversible W (vs. non-self-adjointness of Wds in this geometry) gives a crisp structural explanation for why spectral gap alone does not determine performance. The spectral identities (Proposition C.14, exact norms of the tracking recursion matrices via Kronecker factorization) are carefully derived and avoid window-averaging, yielding more transparent bounds than Koloskova et al. (2021).

The theoretical pipeline is coherent: tight bounds (Theorem 6.5) → spectral condition for Strategy II to win (Theorem 7.1) → interpretable Rayleigh-quotient condition (Theorem 7.2, proved necessary and sufficient) → simple degree–weight edge condition (Corollary 7.3) with a matching argument that proportional degree allocation maximizes the minimum edge coefficient. This gives actionable topology-design guidance, which is uncommon in this literature.

Experiments are consistent with the theory at three scales (16/32/64 nodes, weight ratios up to 50) on both synthetic least-squares and CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, across ring/exp/grid/ER/geometric/tailored topologies; Table 1 empirically supports the degree–weight matching principle (tailored topologies give larger gaps for W than for Wds). The tailored-topology construction (Algorithm 2 with Havel–Hakimi plus degree-preserving swaps and a fallback) is fully specified in Appendix E.

The paper is honest about scope: Remark 6.6 explicitly states the comparison is not a minimax statement or lower bound, Remark 6.8 explains why only one strategy gets a Euclidean-space comparison, and the conclusion acknowledges directed graphs and lower bounds as open. The uniform-weight corollary recovering O(1/√(nT)) confirms consistency with classical results. Appendices contain complete proofs.
weaknesses: The central claim 'row-stochastic matrices can provably outperform' is established only by comparing non-asymptotic upper bounds within a single-loop gradient-tracking algorithm class. There is no lower bound showing Strategy I cannot match these bounds, and the authors themselves concede this (Remark 6.6). An alternative doubly-stochastic algorithm (e.g., with extra communication rounds, as in Liang et al. 2025a/b) might close or reverse the gap, so the practical force of the 'provably outperform' framing is weaker than the title suggests.

The key insight—reversibility/detailed balance makes the mixing operator self-adjoint in the λ-weighted inner product—is standard Markov-chain material, and the diffusion literature (Sayed, 2014; Chen & Sayed, 2013) already implicitly uses this geometry. The novelty is mainly in the comparison and the constant-level analysis rather than a fundamentally new technique; the contribution, while solid, is incremental in analytical tooling.

There is a theory–experiment mismatch: Theorem 7.1 (and the spectral analysis generally) assumes ε ≥ 1/2 to guarantee nonnegative spectra, but the experiments deliberately use ε = 0.3 (Appendix F.2) for larger spectral gaps. The experimental validation of the comparison theorems therefore does not operate exactly in the regime where the theory is stated.

The topology-design guidelines require the ability to construct the network from λ (Algorithm 2), i.e., nodes must know prescribed weights and the topology must be re-designable. In many realistic decentralized deployments the topology is fixed by physical or infrastructure constraints, which limits the applicability of Corollary 7.3; the paper does not discuss this constraint on its guidelines.

Experimental breadth is limited: CIFAR-10 uses vanilla SGD with a single fixed configuration, up to 32 nodes, 6 seeds; no baselines beyond the two in-paper strategies (e.g., push-sum, Exact Diffusion, multi-round communication variants), and no statement about code release, which weakens reproducibility verification of the more complex parts (Algorithm 2, tailored topologies).

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('grpahs', 'obatin', 'definited'), some notational strain in the appendix (e.g., 'σ(P−1π) = {0, σ2(P), …}' with an assertion about (P−Π)v = Pv when πv = 0 needs care for left vs. right eigenvectors; Lemma C.9's descent step uses α ≤ 1/β while Lemma C.17/C.18 use slightly different step-size conditions), and Proposition 6.4/Thm 6.5 constants are heavy, making the head-to-head comparison conditions hard to parse at fixed α and T (which motivates the somewhat loose sufficient condition of Theorem 7.1).
